extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, policymakers, and readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (late 18th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for structuring the executive appointment power and the judiciary (nomination with Senate, tenure 'during good behavior', separation of powers, etc.) as set out in Federalist Papers Nos. 77–79.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination with Senate consent vs sole appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: The President should have the power of nomination while the Senate's concurrence is required for appointment; nomination confers the principal advantages of appointment while avoiding disadvantages of absolute appointment by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomination exercises the President's judgment and responsibility as fully as appointment; the Senate's approval serves as a check without materially diminishing executive accountability. Even if a nomination is sometimes overruled, the ultimate appointee remains the President's choice in a practical sense. This arrangement secures the 'good' of appointment and avoids its evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate concurrence as a check on favoritism and unfit appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring the Senate's concurrence in appointments operates as a powerful (often silent) restraint on presidential favoritism and state-, family-, or popularity-based selections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The possibility of Senate rejection motivates the President to propose qualified candidates and discourages appointments based on personal attachments or political favoritism. The public nature of the process and the Senate's independent discussion increase stability and public confidence in appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of wholesale Senate corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unlikely the Executive could corrupt or purchase the integrity of the whole Senate; a substantial independent and public-spirited portion will resist venality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (e.g., partial venality in the British Commons) show that even in corrupt periods a significant independent element exists. Constitutional provisions (e.g., ineligibility rules preventing senators/officers from certain appointments) further guard against executive influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and public accountability in the appointment process
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments should be conducted in a manner that makes the circumstances and actors publicly known so responsibility for good or bad nominations is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public process ties blame or praise to the President (for nominating) and the Senate (for approving), unlike small secretive councils where responsibility is obscure and cabal/intrigue flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of small private councils for appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Small councils (e.g., three-to-five members) for appointments are improper because they encourage cabal, intrigue, vote-bartering, and monopolization of offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such councils are fewer in number, operate out of public view, are more easily influenced by private attachments, can be manipulated by regulating attendance, and tend to produce unstable and improper appointments—favoring oligarchy over merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuitability of the House of Representatives for making appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The House, being large and subject to frequent change, is an inappropriate body to exercise appointment power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having the House appoint would defeat stability in the Executive and Senate, create infinite delays and embarrassments, and is discouraged by examples in state constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive's remaining discretionary powers (informing, recommending, convening, receiving, executing, commissioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive should retain powers to inform Congress of the state of the Union, recommend measures, convene or adjourn Congress in special cases, receive ambassadors, faithfully execute the laws, and commission officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These authorities are proper and necessary to the energy of the Executive; objections (e.g., about convening or reception of ambassadors) are largely unsubstantial and answered by the relations between Executive and Senate (e.g., treaty concurrence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial tenure during good behavior (permanency) as essential to independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should hold office during good behavior (essentially permanent tenure) to secure an independent judiciary capable of defending rights and the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanency protects the judiciary from encroachments by the Executive and Legislature, enables judges to resist popular 'ill humors,' and helps ensure faithful performance of duties. Temporary or frequently renewed commissions would compromise independence through susceptibility to influence from appointing authorities or popularity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary as the weakest department requiring safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the judiciary has neither the sword (force) nor the purse (money), it is the weakest branch and therefore needs safeguards (like permanency) to defend itself and the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judiciary depends on the executive for enforcement and on law for authority; its weakness makes permanency and independence essential so it can serve as an effective check and protector of constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts as interpreters and guardians of the Constitution (power to declare statutes void)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must be able to judge whether legislative acts conform to the Constitution; when a statute contradicts the Constitution, it is void and courts should prefer the Constitution over statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not imply judicial superiority over the legislature but recognizes the people's will (the Constitution) as superior to agents' statutes. Courts function as an intermediate body between the people and the legislature to keep statutes within constitutional bounds. Rules of construction (e.g., preferring later acts among equals) are tools but subordinate to constitutional supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritizing superior authority in conflicts (constitutional primacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: When laws from superior and subordinate authorities conflict, the prior act of the superior (the Constitution) should be preferred to subsequent acts of the inferior (the legislature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among equal authorities courts may prefer the last in time, but between superior and subordinate the reason of the thing dictates following the superior (constitutional) provision. This is a foundation for judicial review and constitutional guardianship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for permanency to attract and maintain qualified judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanency of judicial office is necessary because the body of laws and precedents is voluminous and requires long study; temporary tenure would discourage skilled practitioners from accepting the bench.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because only a few persons can acquire the required skill and integrity, temporary duration would lead to less able administration of justice and reduce the pool of qualified candidates, harming the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence as a check on legislative injustice and fluctuating public passions
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent judiciary moderates immediate harms from momentary popular prejudices and unjust, partial laws by confining their operation and deterring their passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts' firmness mitigates the effects of transient public 'ill humors,' operates as a preventative influence on legislatures considering iniquitous measures, and protects minority rights until the people can use constitutional means to alter the law.
